did_you_know.text: The LORD presents his servant as his chosen one, upon whom his Spirit rests, whose task is to bring justice to the nations.
The servant acts without noise or force: he will not shout, raise his voice, or make it heard in the streets.
The images of the bruised reed and the dimly burning wick convey a gentle, strengthening attitude toward the weak and vulnerable; the servant will not break or extinguish them.
The servant’s work is described as persevering until justice is established on earth, and the islands await his teaching.
The LORD is described as the Creator of the heavens and the earth, and as the one who gives breath and spirit to all living things on the earth.
The servant’s mission includes being a covenant for the people and a light to the nations, as well as opening blind eyes and bringing prisoners out of dungeons and darkness.
The LORD emphasizes his uniqueness: he will not give his glory to another or his praise to idols.
The new song to the LORD reaches to the ends of the earth: those who go down to the sea, the islands, and their inhabitants are all called to join in the praise.
In the description of redemption, the LORD is compared to a mighty warrior and a man of war who goes out and acts powerfully against his enemies.

In the latter part of the chapter, Israel is called a blind and deaf servant, even though it has seen much and heard much; this highlights the gap between the ability to perceive and actually listening.
